overview.text: Geothermal energy is heat from within Earth, accessed from hot rocks, underground water or steam, and—in heating and cooling systems—the relatively steady temperature of shallow ground. Its significance is its versatility: deep geothermal fluids can be brought up through wells and used to turn turbines and generate electricity, while direct-use systems supply heat to buildings or industrial processes. Geothermal heat pumps work differently: they exchange heat with the ground, drawing it into buildings in winter and transferring indoor heat into the ground in summer. Electricity plants include dry-steam, flash-steam, and binary-cycle designs. Earth’s interior heat is continually replenished by the natural decay of radioactive elements.

key_facts.text: “Geothermal” means heat from Earth; geothermal resources include hot rocks and underground water or steam.
In geothermal power plants, underground heat reaches the surface through wells and is used to drive turbines that generate electricity.
Dry-steam, flash-steam, and binary-cycle plants use different methods to turn geothermal heat into turbine power.
Geothermal heat pumps use the ground’s relatively steady temperature: they bring heat indoors in winter and move indoor heat into the ground in summer.
Geothermal heat can also be used directly for building heat and industrial processes, without first generating electricity.
